scaleInfo.name: Dorian Mode
scaleInfo.character: Sophisticated, modern, jazzy minor with a bright natural 6th

relativeScale.name: Major Scale
relativeScale.intervalDistance: Major 2nd above the major root (D Dorian = C Major)

keyExamples.notes: D - E - F - G - A - B - C - D
keyExamples.commonUse: Most common dorian key, parent scale is C major, starting on D

keyExamples.notes: E - F# - G - A - B - C# - D - E
keyExamples.commonUse: Natural guitar key, great for open position playing

keyExamples.notes: A - B - C - D - E - F# - G - A
keyExamples.commonUse: Popular rock key, parent scale is G major

keyExamples.notes: B - C# - D - E - F# - G# - A - B
keyExamples.commonUse: Jazz-friendly key, great for higher position playing

patterns.description: Natural fingering in open position, easy transition from D minor shapes. Perfect for folk and Celtic styles.
patterns.fretDiagram: Uses open strings and first 3 frets on strings 4-1

patterns.description: Popular rock position, moveable pattern for all keys. Most versatile for improvisation.
Jazz-friendly position with comfortable fingering for complex lines and chord melody playing

diatonicChords.function: Tonic - Home chord, minor center with sophistication
Subdominant - Characteristic dorian chord (major IV in minor key)
Dominant - Minor dominant, softer resolution than major V
Submediant - Tension chord, leads to resolution
Subtonic - Modal cadence chord, strong resolution to tonic

commonProgressions.name: Dorian Vamp (i-IV)
commonProgressions.description: The signature dorian progression, highlighting the major IV chord over minor tonic. The defining sound of dorian mode.

commonProgressions.name: Modal Minor (i-♭VII-IV-i)
commonProgressions.description: Extended dorian progression with subtonic chord movement, common in rock and progressive music

commonProgressions.name: Jazz Dorian (i7-ii7-i7-IV7)
commonProgressions.description: Jazz-style dorian progression with 7th chord extensions for sophisticated harmonic movement

commonProgressions.name: Suspended Dorian (i-IV-♭VII)
commonProgressions.description: Modal vamp using the three major chords available in dorian, creates an open, floating sound

genreApplications.usage: Essential jazz mode for minor 7th chords and ii-V-I progressions
Modern and progressive rock solos with a sophisticated minor sound
examples: Another Brick in the Wall - Pink Floyd

genreApplications.usage: Traditional Celtic and Irish music extensively uses dorian tonality
Funky minor grooves built on the dorian i-IV vamp
Jazz-rock fusion with complex dorian harmonies and improvisations

practiceExercises.name: D Dorian Scale Runs
practiceExercises.description: Practice the D dorian scale ascending and descending in open position
instructions: Start slowly with metronome at 60 BPM
Listen for the natural 6th (B note) that defines the dorian sound
Gradually increase tempo as accuracy improves

practiceExercises.name: Dorian Modal Sequences
practiceExercises.description: Practice dorian in thirds to hear the modal character and intervallic relationships
instructions: Practice intervals systematically through the scale
Listen carefully to the dorian thirds pattern
Use alternate picking for even articulation
Work on smooth transitions between string crossings

practiceExercises.name: Jazz Dorian Phrase
practiceExercises.description: Simple dorian phrase over Dm7 chord with jazz phrasing and musical expression
instructions: Play over a Dm7 backing track or chord vamp
Focus on musical phrasing, not just notes
Emphasize the natural 6th for dorian color
Experiment with rhythmic variations and dynamics

practiceExercises.name: Dorian vs Natural Minor Ear Training
practiceExercises.description: Compare dorian with natural minor to hear the characteristic raised 6th that defines the mode
instructions: Play dorian scale, then natural minor back to back
Focus on the 6th degree difference (B natural vs B flat in D)
Sing both scales to internalize the difference
Identify dorian by its brighter, more sophisticated minor character

relatedScales.differences: Dorian has a natural 6th instead of flat 6th - this is the only difference
relatedScales.usage: Darker, more traditional minor sound compared to dorian's brightness

relatedScales.differences: Dorian is the 2nd mode of the major scale; same notes, different tonal center
relatedScales.usage: D Dorian uses the same notes as C Major but centers on D

relatedScales.differences: Mixolydian is a major mode with flat 7th; dorian is a minor mode with natural 6th
relatedScales.usage: Dominant flavor, works over 7th chords in blues and rock

relatedScales.differences: Phrygian has a flat 2nd, creating a Spanish/exotic flavor vs dorian's sophistication
relatedScales.usage: Spanish-flavored minor mode, darker and more exotic than dorian

relatedScales.differences: Uses 5 notes from dorian (1, b3, 4, 5, b7), omitting the characteristic 2nd and 6th
relatedScales.usage: Simplified version for soloing, can be extended to full dorian for color
